questions.title: Embedded Tomcat
questions.question: What is embedded Tomcat and how does it work in Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Tomcat is included in the JAR:** packaged inside the fat JAR, not external
- **`spring-boot-starter-web` includes it by default:** zero explicit configuration needed
- **Advantage over WAR deployment:** self-contained, consistent across environments
- **Port 8080 default:** `server.port` to change
- **Red flag:** not knowing why embedded server changed the deployment model (no WAR, no app server config)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Embedded Tomcat is a fully functional Servlet container packaged inside your Spring Boot application JAR. When you include `spring-boot-starter-web`, Spring Boot auto-configures and starts Tomcat as part of the application startup — no external Tomcat installation required.

This fundamentally changed Java deployment. Before Spring Boot, you'd package a WAR file and deploy it to an already-running Tomcat instance. With embedded Tomcat, your application is `java -jar app.jar` — portable, consistent, and deployable anywhere a JVM runs. The same artifact runs on a developer's laptop and in production without environment-specific configuration of an external server.

Spring Boot starts Tomcat programmatically using `TomcatServletWebServerFactory`, registers the Spring DispatcherServlet into Tomcat's servlet context, and Tomcat begins accepting HTTP connections. From the outside, it's indistinguishable from a traditional Tomcat deployment.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Embedded Tomcat is a fully functional Servlet container packaged inside your Spring Boot application JAR.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: From the outside, it's indistinguishable from a traditional Tomcat deployment.

questions.title: Switching to Undertow
questions.question: How do you switch from embedded Tomcat to Undertow?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat`, add `spring-boot-starter-undertow`:** the exact change
- **Why Undertow?** non-blocking I/O, lower memory footprint, no Permgen issues pre-Java 8
- **Same properties namespace:** `server.*` works identically for both servers
- **Undertow-specific config:** `server.undertow.*` for fine-tuning
- **Red flag:** not knowing you must explicitly exclude Tomcat — just adding Undertow doesn't remove Tomcat

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Switching from Tomcat to Undertow is a two-step dependency change. First, you exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web`. Then you add `spring-boot-starter-undertow` as a dependency. Spring Boot's auto-configuration detects the absence of Tomcat and presence of Undertow and configures Undertow instead.

You can't simply add Undertow without excluding Tomcat — both would be on the classpath and Spring Boot would still use Tomcat by default. The exclusion is mandatory.

Undertow's advantages include lower memory usage, a non-blocking architecture that handles more connections per thread, and often better throughput at high concurrency. The trade-off is that Undertow is less familiar to operations teams and has a smaller ecosystem of documentation compared to Tomcat.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Maven Configuration

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Gradle Configuration

```groovy
configurations {
    all*.exclude group: 'org.springframework.boot', module: 'spring-boot-starter-tomcat'
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web'
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-undertow'
}
```

## Undertow-Specific Properties

```properties
# Worker threads (handles request processing)
server.undertow.threads.worker=200

# I/O threads (handles I/O — typically set to CPU count)
server.undertow.threads.io=4

# Buffer size
server.undertow.buffer-size=1024

# Access log
server.undertow.accesslog.enabled=true
server.undertow.accesslog.pattern=combined
```

## Comparison: Tomcat vs Undertow vs Jetty

| | Tomcat | Undertow | Jetty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | NIO + threads | Non-blocking I/O | NIO |
| Memory | Medium | Low | Low |
| Ecosystem | Largest | Growing | Large |
| WebSocket | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Servlet 5.0 | Yes | Yes | Yes |

## Production Reality

Switch to Undertow when you have benchmarks showing it improves your specific workload. For typical CRUD applications, the difference is negligible. Undertow genuinely shines in scenarios with many long-lived connections (WebSockets, SSE) or extremely high concurrent connections — situations where Tomcat's thread-per-request model creates overhead.

speakable_v2.hook: Switching from Tomcat to Undertow is a two-step dependency change.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The trade-off is that Undertow is less familiar to operations teams and has a smaller ecosystem of documentation compared to Tomcat.

questions.title: Embedded Server Customization
questions.question: How do you customize embedded server settings programmatically?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`WebServerFactoryCustomizer<T>`:** the hook for programmatic customization
- **`TomcatServletWebServerFactory`:** the concrete factory for Tomcat-specific config
- **Why programmatic?** when properties aren't expressive enough (e.g., adding custom connectors)
- **`@Bean` registration:** customizer is just a Spring bean
- **Red flag:** not knowing there's a programmatic API beyond properties

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For customizations not expressible via `application.properties`, Spring Boot provides `WebServerFactoryCustomizer<T>`. You implement this interface, annotate the class with `@Component`, and Spring Boot calls it with the server factory before starting the server.

The generic type `T` determines which server type you're customizing. `WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory>` gives you access to Tomcat-specific APIs — adding extra HTTP connectors, configuring SSL programmatically, adding Tomcat Valve components for request processing.

A common use case is adding an HTTP connector alongside an HTTPS connector — something that's complex to express in properties but straightforward with the factory API. Another use case is adding a Tomcat `AccessLogValve` with custom log format and log rotation settings.

speakable_v2.hook: For customizations not expressible via application.properties, Spring Boot provides WebServerFactoryCustomizer<T>.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Another use case is adding a Tomcat AccessLogValve with custom log format and log rotation settings.

questions.title: SSL/TLS Configuration
questions.question: How do you configure SSL/TLS for an embedded server in Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`server.ssl.*` properties:** the property namespace for SSL
- **Key store types:** JKS, PKCS12 — Spring Boot 2.7+ prefers PKCS12
- **`server.port=443` or `8443`:** HTTPS requires changing the port
- **Certificate sources:** keystore file, classpath, or programmatic for cloud secrets
- **Red flag:** not knowing the difference between keystore (your cert) and truststore (trusted CAs)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
SSL configuration in Spring Boot is done via the `server.ssl.*` property namespace. You specify the path to your keystore file, the keystore type (PKCS12 is preferred now), the keystore password, and the key alias. Spring Boot wires this into the embedded server's HTTPS connector.

For HTTPS you also need to change `server.port` to 443 or 8443, since Tomcat will only listen for HTTPS on the configured port after SSL is set up.

In production, managing keystores directly in properties files is fragile. A better approach is to terminate SSL at a load balancer or ingress controller — your Spring Boot app runs plain HTTP internally and the load balancer handles the certificate. This is simpler to manage certificates (renew at the load balancer level) and removes SSL overhead from your application servers.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: SSL configuration in Spring Boot is done via the server.ssl.* property namespace.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is simpler to manage certificates (renew at the load balancer level) and removes SSL overhead from your application servers.

questions.title: Graceful Shutdown
questions.question: How does Spring Boot implement graceful shutdown?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`server.shutdown=graceful`:** the single property to enable it (Boot 2.3+)
- **What happens:** stops accepting new requests, waits for in-flight requests to finish
- **Timeout:** `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` — default 30 seconds
- **Kubernetes integration:** pair with `preStop` hook and termination grace period
- **Red flag:** not knowing it was added in Boot 2.3 — many codebases are on earlier versions

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.3 introduced built-in graceful shutdown via `server.shutdown=graceful`. When the JVM receives a SIGTERM — like when Kubernetes sends a pod termination signal — the embedded server stops accepting new incoming requests but waits for any currently in-flight requests to complete before shutting down.

The timeout for waiting is controlled by `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`, defaulting to 30 seconds. If in-flight requests don't complete within that timeout, the shutdown proceeds anyway to prevent indefinite blocking.

In Kubernetes, you pair this with a `preStop` hook that sleeps for a few seconds. This accounts for the time between Kubernetes sending SIGTERM and actually removing the pod from the load balancer endpoints — without the sleep, some requests might still be routed to your pod during that window.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Configuration

```properties
# Enable graceful shutdown (Boot 2.3+)
server.shutdown=graceful

# Maximum wait time for in-flight requests
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s
```

## Shutdown Sequence

```
1. SIGTERM received
2. Readiness probe starts failing (pod removed from load balancer)
3. Spring stops accepting new HTTP requests
4. Waits up to timeout for in-flight requests to complete
5. Spring context shutdown hooks run (@PreDestroy, DisposableBean)
6. JVM exits
```

## Kubernetes Integration

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]  # Allow LB to drain
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60  # Must be > timeout-per-shutdown-phase
```

The `preStop` sleep and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` must be larger than `timeout-per-shutdown-phase` or Kubernetes will SIGKILL the process before graceful shutdown completes.

## Monitoring Shutdown

```java
@Component
public class ShutdownListener {
    @PreDestroy
    public void onShutdown() {
        log.info("Application shutting down - cleaning up resources");
        // Flush metrics, close connections, etc.
    }
}
```

## Production Reality

Graceful shutdown is essential for zero-downtime deployments. Without it, rolling deployments drop requests being processed when a pod terminates. With `server.shutdown=graceful`, the pod finishes what it's doing before dying. The combination of graceful shutdown + readiness probe + `preStop` hook is the standard pattern for production Kubernetes deployments.

questions.title: Fat JAR / Uber JAR
questions.question: What is a fat JAR in Spring Boot and how is it created?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Definition:** all dependencies + your code in one executable JAR
- **`spring-boot-maven-plugin`:** the Maven plugin that builds it
- **`java -jar app.jar`:** how you run it
- **Difference from regular JAR:** regular JARs can't include other JARs in a classpath-compatible way — Spring Boot uses nested JARs
- **Red flag:** not knowing the embedded server is also inside the fat JAR

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A fat JAR — also called an uber JAR or executable JAR — is a single JAR file that contains your application code, all its dependencies, and the embedded server. You can distribute and run it with `java -jar app.jar` on any machine with a JVM.

The `spring-boot-maven-plugin` (or Gradle equivalent) builds it with `mvn package`. Spring Boot's approach is unique: instead of unpacking dependency JARs and repackaging their class files — which causes class name conflicts — it uses a custom nested JAR loader that keeps dependency JARs intact inside the fat JAR.

This changes the deployment story entirely. You no longer need to install and configure an application server on each machine. The same artifact that developers run locally is what goes to production, eliminating "works on my machine" issues from server configuration differences.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Building the Fat JAR

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

```bash
mvn clean package
# Output: target/myapp-1.0.0.jar  (~50-80MB with all dependencies)
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar
```

## Fat JAR Structure

```
myapp.jar
├── BOOT-INF/
│   ├── classes/          (your compiled classes)
│   │   └── com/example/*.class
│   └── lib/              (dependency JARs — kept intact)
│       ├── spring-core-6.x.jar
│       ├── hibernate-core-6.x.jar
│       └── ... (100+ JARs)
├── META-INF/
│   └── MANIFEST.MF       (Main-Class: JarLauncher)
└── org/springframework/boot/loader/
    └── JarLauncher.class (Spring's custom class loader)
```

## Excluding Dev Dependencies

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <excludes>
            <exclude>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
            </exclude>
        </excludes>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

## Production Reality

Fat JARs work well for most deployments but can be slow to push over the network (50-80MB per release). For containerised deployments, consider layered JARs — Spring Boot 2.3+ supports building Docker images with separate layers for dependencies and application code. Dependencies rarely change, so Docker only pushes the small application layer on each release.

speakable_v2.hook: A fat JAR — also called an uber JAR or executable JAR — is a single JAR file that contains your application code, all its dependencies, and the embedded server.
speakable_v2.cap: The same artifact that developers run locally is what goes to production, eliminating "works on my machine" issues from server configuration differences.

questions.title: WebServerFactory
questions.question: What is WebServerFactory and how is it used in Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Factory pattern:** `WebServerFactory` creates the embedded server instance
- **Concrete implementations:** `TomcatServletWebServerFactory`, `UndertowServletWebServerFactory`, `JettyServletWebServerFactory`
- **`WebServerFactoryCustomizer`:** the preferred way to modify factory settings as a bean
- **`@Bean` override:** you can replace the entire factory for full control
- **Red flag:** not knowing the factory is what auto-configuration creates — you're modifying the factory, not the server directly

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`WebServerFactory` is the abstraction that creates and configures the embedded web server. Spring Boot's auto-configuration creates the appropriate concrete factory — `TomcatServletWebServerFactory`, `UndertowServletWebServerFactory`, or `JettyServletWebServerFactory` — based on what's on the classpath.

You interact with the factory in two ways. The simpler way is `WebServerFactoryCustomizer<T>`, where you receive the auto-configured factory and tweak its settings. The more powerful way is replacing the factory bean entirely — you declare a `@Bean` of the factory type, and your bean takes precedence over the auto-configured one, giving you complete control.

Replace the factory only when you need deep configuration that the customizer API doesn't expose — like setting up a completely custom connector architecture. For most use cases, properties and the customizer interface are sufficient.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: WebServerFactory is the abstraction that creates and configures the embedded web server.
speakable_v2.cap: For most use cases, properties and the customizer interface are sufficient.

questions.title: Response Compression
questions.question: How do you enable response compression in Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`server.compression.enabled=true`:** the single property
- **Minimum response size:** don't compress small responses — compression overhead exceeds savings
- **MIME types:** configure which content types to compress
- **Gzip is default algorithm:** deflate also available
- **Red flag:** not knowing compression at the load balancer is often preferred

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Enabling response compression in Spring Boot is a one-liner: `server.compression.enabled=true`. This configures the embedded server to compress HTTP responses using gzip when the client sends an `Accept-Encoding: gzip` header.

Two important companion settings: `server.compression.min-response-size` controls the minimum response body size before compression is applied — the default is 2KB, which is sensible since compressing tiny responses adds CPU overhead for negligible bandwidth savings. `server.compression.mime-types` lists which content types get compressed — typically JSON, HTML, CSS, JavaScript but not binary formats like images or PDFs, which are already compressed.

In production, compression is often better handled at the load balancer or CDN level. Nginx, AWS ALB, and Cloudflare can all compress responses and have hardware-optimised compression. This offloads CPU from your application servers and allows compression configuration to be managed at the infrastructure layer.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Configuration

```properties
# Enable compression
server.compression.enabled=true

# Minimum size to compress (default: 2048 bytes)
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# MIME types to compress (defaults cover common cases)
server.compression.mime-types=application/json,application/xml,text/html,text/plain,text/css,application/javascript

# Excluded user agents (some old browsers have gzip bugs)
# server.compression.excluded-user-agents=
```

## What Compression Does

| Content Type | Original | Compressed | Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| JSON API response | 100KB | 15KB | 85% |
| HTML page | 50KB | 8KB | 84% |
| CSS bundle | 200KB | 40KB | 80% |
| JPEG image | 500KB | 498KB | ~0% |

Images, audio, and video are already compressed — don't include them.

## Verifying Compression

```bash
curl -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" -v http://localhost:8080/api/data 2>&1 | grep content-encoding
# Should show: content-encoding: gzip
```

## Production Reality

For static assets served via CDN (Cloudflare, CloudFront), compression at the application level is redundant — the CDN handles it and caches compressed versions. Enable application-level compression only for dynamic API responses that bypass the CDN cache. Measure actual CPU impact on your instances before enabling globally — on CPU-constrained application servers, compression can add meaningful overhead.

speakable_v2.hook: Enabling response compression in Spring Boot is a one-liner: server.compression.enabled=true.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This offloads CPU from your application servers and allows compression configuration to be managed at the infrastructure layer.

questions.title: Multipart File Upload Configuration
questions.question: How do you configure file upload handling in Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`spring.servlet.multipart.*` namespace:** the configuration prefix
- **`max-file-size` vs `max-request-size`:** single file vs total request limits
- **`MultipartFile` in controller:** how you receive files in Spring MVC
- **Streaming large files:** don't load into memory — stream to destination
- **Red flag:** setting file size limits without knowing what they default to (1MB file, 10MB request)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
File upload configuration lives under `spring.servlet.multipart.*`. The two most important properties are `max-file-size` — the maximum size for a single file, defaulting to 1MB — and `max-request-size` — the total size of the multipart request including all files and form fields, defaulting to 10MB.

In your controller, you receive uploaded files as `MultipartFile` parameters annotated with `@RequestParam`. For single files it's straightforward; for multiple files you accept a `List<MultipartFile>`.

The critical consideration for production is memory. `MultipartFile.getBytes()` loads the entire file into heap memory. For files over a few megabytes, use `MultipartFile.transferTo(File)` or stream directly to your storage service using `MultipartFile.getInputStream()`. Loading a 50MB file into memory in a request handler is a quick path to OutOfMemoryError under concurrent upload load.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: File upload configuration lives under spring.servlet.multipart.*.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Loading a 50MB file into memory in a request handler is a quick path to OutOfMemoryError under concurrent upload load.

questions.title: Reactive Server with WebFlux
questions.question: How does the embedded server change when using Spring WebFlux?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Netty is default for WebFlux:** not Tomcat
- **Non-blocking:** one thread handles many requests via event loop, not thread-per-request
- **Reactive stack requires `spring-boot-starter-webflux`:** separate from `spring-boot-starter-web`
- **Can still use Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow:** they support Reactive Streams as well
- **Red flag:** mixing `spring-boot-starter-web` and `spring-boot-starter-webflux` — they conflict

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When you use Spring WebFlux instead of Spring MVC, the default embedded server changes from Tomcat to Netty. Netty uses a non-blocking event loop architecture — a small number of threads handle thousands of concurrent connections by using callbacks and asynchronous I/O instead of blocking one thread per request.

To use WebFlux, you replace `spring-boot-starter-web` with `spring-boot-starter-webflux`. Spring Boot's auto-configuration detects the change and starts a `ReactiveWebServerFactory` — by default `NettyReactiveWebServerFactory` — instead of the Servlet-based Tomcat factory.

The key implication is your entire application must be reactive end-to-end. If you use blocking code — traditional JDBC, synchronous file I/O, blocking method calls — inside reactive handlers, you block the event loop thread and lose all the concurrency benefits. The reactive model shines when your workload is genuinely I/O-bound with high concurrency and you use reactive clients like R2DBC for databases and `WebClient` for HTTP calls.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Dependency Change

```xml
<!-- Remove this -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Add this -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Thread Model Comparison

| | Spring MVC + Tomcat | Spring WebFlux + Netty |
|---|---|---|
| Default server | Tomcat | Netty |
| Thread model | Thread per request | Event loop |
| Default threads | 200 | 2 × CPU cores |
| Programming model | Imperative | Reactive (Mono/Flux) |
| Best for | Standard CRUD | High concurrency, streaming |

## Netty Configuration

```properties
# For WebFlux + Netty:
server.netty.connection-timeout=20s
server.netty.idle-timeout=60s
server.netty.max-keep-alive-requests=200
```

## Using Tomcat with WebFlux

If you need WebFlux but prefer Tomcat:
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>io.projectreactor.netty</groupId>
            <artifactId>reactor-netty-http</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<!-- Add tomcat reactive -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Production Reality

Don't adopt WebFlux just for theoretical performance gains. If your team writes blocking code (JDBC, synchronous REST calls), WebFlux can be worse than MVC — blocking the event loop is more damaging than blocking a dedicated request thread. Use WebFlux when you have genuinely high concurrency requirements and the whole team is comfortable with reactive programming.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The reactive model shines when your workload is genuinely I/O-bound with high concurrency and you use reactive clients like R2DBC for databases and WebClient for HTTP calls.
